title: Lower Complexity Bounds for Nonconvex-Strongly-Convex Bilevel Optimization with First-Order Oracles
claim: The hard instance forces progress through a chain, where each coordinate update needs a specific oracle type in strict sequence.
layout: Legend box top-left, one horizontal chain left-to-right, vertical arrows above nodes
description: A single horizontal chain diagram on white background. A gray legend box at top-left maps arrow colors to oracle types: blue for the gradient of g with respect to y-tilde, green for the gradient of g with respect to x, and red for the gradient of f. Along the bottom, nodes y_1^(i), y_2^(i), ..., y_{n-1}^(i), y_n^(i) are joined by blue arrows, with small blue arrow fragments standing in for the omitted middle nodes. A red arrow leads from y_n^(i) to y_1^(i+1), and the next block repeats the same pattern. Green vertical arrows rise from y_n^(i) and y_n^(i+1) to x_i and x_{i+1}. The eye goes first to the colored arrows, then follows the chain left to right.
caption: An illustration of the zero-chain for our constructed instance in [ref] for nonconvex-strongly-convex bilevel optimization.
abstract: Although upper bound guarantees for bilevel optimization have been widely studied, progress on lower bounds has been limited due to the complexity of the bilevel structure. In this work, we focus on the smooth nonconvex-strongly-convex setting and develop new hard instances that yield nontrivial lower bounds under deterministic and stochastic first-order oracle models. In the deterministic case, we prove that any first-order zero-respecting algorithm requires at least $Î©(Îº^{3/2}Îµ^{-2})$ oracle calls to find an $Îµ$-accurate stationary point, improving the optimal lower bounds known for single-level nonconvex optimization and for nonconvex-strongly-convex min-max problems. In the stochastic case, we show that at least $Î©(Îº^{5/2}Îµ^{-4})$ stochastic oracle calls are necessary, again strengthening the best known bounds in related settings. Our results expose substantial gaps between current upper and lower bounds for bilevel optimization and suggest that even simplified regimes, such as those with quadratic lower-level objectives, warrant further investigation toward understanding the optimal complexity of bilevel optimization under standard first-order oracles.
